article.headline: The Web Gets Photorealistic 3D Worlds, 20 Years After Second Life
article.lede: Robert Scoble's passing reference to Microsoft's mid-2000s Second Life experiments frames a genuinely significant technical announcement: Spark 2.0, an open-source JavaScript library that can stream photorealistic three-dimensional scenes containing 100 million or more elements to any device — phones included — using only a browser's native graphics layer. The gap between what was imaginable in 2005 and what is buildable today is the actual subject.
article.body:
The substance of the post lives in @sparkjsdev's announcement, not Scoble's frame. Spark 2.0 is built on Three.js — the web's most widely used 3D rendering library — and centers on *3D Gaussian Splatting*, a technique that represents a scene not as polygon meshes (the geometry of games and CAD software) but as millions of semi-transparent ellipsoids, each "splat" statistically fitted to photographs or video of real spaces. The results can be strikingly photorealistic, capturing surface texture in ways that traditional mesh rendering requires enormous artist effort to approximate.

The engineering challenge the library addresses is delivery at scale. A raw scene of 100 million splats is a very large dataset; sending it all before the user sees anything is impractical. Spark 2.0's answer is a **streamable Level-of-Detail (LoD)** system: it transmits a coarse version of the scene first, then progressively refines it as more data arrives — the same principle used in progressive JPEG encoding, extended to three spatial dimensions. The system runs on WebGL2, the graphics API built into every modern browser, requiring no plugin and no app download.

Scoble's Second Life reference is more than nostalgia. Linden Lab launched its virtual world in 2003; it peaked in the late 2000s with millions of users and genuine cultural attention, with corporations — Microsoft among them — holding meetings and product launches inside it, per BBC reporting. That episode established real appetite for persistent shared virtual spaces but stalled on fidelity and accessibility: the blocky visuals and steep learning curve made it a curiosity rather than a destination.

The "**Holodeck**" comparison Scoble invokes is aspirational shorthand, not a technical claim. What Spark 2.0 actually delivers is a compelling browser-based viewer for photorealistic 3D captures — a meaningful step, not a destination. Content pipelines (how ordinary users create and publish splat worlds) and social infrastructure remain underdeveloped. That said, running 100-million-splat scenes on a mobile phone's browser, with open-source code anyone can build on, is a different order of capability than anything Second Life's era could manage.

concepts.definition: A technique for representing three-dimensional scenes using millions of semi-transparent ellipsoids — "splats" — each derived from photographs or video of a real space. Unlike traditional polygon meshes, splats can reproduce photorealistic surface texture with high fidelity and relatively little manual authoring. The method attracted wide attention after a 2023 academic paper showed it could produce real-time, photo-quality renderings.

A technique that delivers a simplified version of a scene immediately, then progressively adds detail as more data arrives — minimizing how long a user waits before seeing anything. Common in game engines and geographic mapping (Google Maps uses it for 3D terrain), it is now being applied to web-based photorealistic 3D content.

A browser API that gives JavaScript programs direct access to a device's GPU for hardware-accelerated 3D graphics, with no plugin required. It is the standard rendering layer for demanding web applications and is supported across all major browsers on desktop, mobile, and VR headsets.

article.fact_check: Scoble's claim that Microsoft ran a virtual world in Second Life approximately 20 years ago is consistent with the platform's timeline — Linden Lab launched Second Life in 2003 and corporate presences were common during its late-2000s peak, per BBC reporting — though the specific Microsoft project is not verified by the provided sources. Spark 2.0's technical specifications (100M+ splats, mobile-to-VR support) come from the developer's own announcement; no independent benchmark is available in the sources here.
